steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper comparing YouTube Shorts with regular videos in terms of user engagement and content creation. Set up the rise of short-form video and the debate around it, state our main question and research questions, describe the dataset briefly, summarize the main findings, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Rise of short-form video
- short-form video content widely popular in last few years
- TikTok: launched 2016, short videos, commercial success; 3 billion downloads, 1 billion active monthly users in 2023
- YouTube, Instagram, Facebook followed with similar formats
- YouTube Shorts: beta in US March 18, 2021; worldwide a few months later; more and more creators adopt it

2. Debate
- lively discussion, spectrum of perspectives
- pros: concise attractive content for creators; disseminating info about social issues; new professional perspectives for creators
- concerns from TikTok studies: dependency, increase of daytime fatigue, decrease of prospective memory
- impact on informative content (educational videos, depth and detail) should be explored
- main question: "Are short videos replacing longer videos on YouTube, the most popular online video-sharing platform?"

3. Our study
- first comprehensive study of YouTube Shorts vs regular videos (RVs): channel behavior and user engagement
- public YouTube Data API; control for platform, creator, video features
- longitudinal comparative analysis, two years after March 2021 introduction
- insights for content creators, advertisers, researchers
- RQ1: effect on preexisting channels' content creation; new channels vs older ones
- RQ2: Shorts vs RVs, views and creation frequency across categories
- RQ3: engagement differences (views, likes, comments); influence of RV duration

4. Dataset
- 70k channels with at least one Shorts since March 2021
- 9.9M Shorts, 6.9M RVs, January 2021 - December 2022
- per video: category, views, likes, comments

5. Findings
- channels posting a Short tend to adopt format, eventually more Shorts than RVs
- categories uneven: Shorts mainly entertainment; RVs wide variety incl. political, educational -> co-exist for different purposes
- political, educational, artistic Shorts get fewer views -> viewers prefer RVs for some categories
- Shorts outperform RVs in views and likes per view, fewer comments per view, gap narrowing
- same channel: Shorts 110 times more views on average
- RVs of 10 to 30 minutes: median views higher than median Shorts views

6. Organization
- Section 2 data; 3 publishing behavior; 4 content differences; 5 engagement; 6 discussion; 7 prior literature; 8 conclusion, limitations, future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, short-form video content has become very popular. TikTok, which is a social media platform focused on short videos launched in 2016, quickly became a commercial success, with 3 billion downloads and 1 billion active monthly users in 2023. Shortly after that, platforms like YouTube, Instagram and Facebook introduced their own short-form video content features, with a similar format on all the platforms. YouTube in particular introduced its format, called Shorts, as a beta version in the US on March 18, 2021, and then worldwide a few months later. Since it was introduced on YouTube, more and more content creators have started making content in this format.

Short-form video content is currently a topic of lively discussion, and there are a lot of different perspectives. On one side, it gives creators an opportunity to engage and entertain their audience with content that is concise and attractive. Short-form videos can also be effective for spreading information about social issues and they create new professional perspectives for content creators. On the other side, recent studies about TikTok pointed out some aspects that may be concerning for its users, like a form of dependency, more daytime fatigue and less prospective memory. Also, its impact on informative content, for example educational videos that depend on depth and detail, should be explored. To look into this, we focus on a fundamental research question: "Are short videos replacing longer videos on YouTube, the most popular online video-sharing platform?"

[Our study]
- first comprehensive study of Shorts vs regular videos (RVs): channel behavior, user engagement
- YouTube Data API; control for platform, creator, video features
- longitudinal, two years after March 2021
- creators, advertisers, researchers
- RQ1 preexisting vs new channels; RQ2 views and frequency across categories; RQ3 engagement, RV duration

[Dataset]
- 70k channels, 9.9M Shorts, 6.9M RVs, January 2021 - December 2022; category, views, likes, comments

[Findings]
- adoption of Shorts; uneven categories; fewer views for political/educational/artistic Shorts
- views and likes per view higher for Shorts, comments per view lower but narrowing; 110 times more views within same channel; 10 to 30 minute RVs higher median

[Organization]
- Sections 2-8

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, short-form video content has become very popular. TikTok, which is a social media platform focused on short videos launched in 2016, quickly became a commercial success, with 3 billion downloads and 1 billion active monthly users in 2023. Shortly after that, platforms like YouTube, Instagram and Facebook introduced their own short-form video content features, with a similar format on all the platforms. YouTube in particular introduced its format, called Shorts, as a beta version in the US on March 18, 2021, and then worldwide a few months later. Since it was introduced on YouTube, more and more content creators have started making content in this format.

Short-form video content is currently a topic of lively discussion, and there are a lot of different perspectives. On one side, it gives creators an opportunity to engage and entertain their audience with content that is concise and attractive. Short-form videos can also be effective for spreading information about social issues and they create new professional perspectives for content creators. On the other side, recent studies about TikTok pointed out some aspects that may be concerning for its users, like a form of dependency, more daytime fatigue and less prospective memory. Also, its impact on informative content, for example educational videos that depend on depth and detail, should be explored. To look into this, we focus on a fundamental research question: "Are short videos replacing longer videos on YouTube, the most popular online video-sharing platform?"

To answer this question, we do the first comprehensive study of YouTube Shorts and compare them with regular videos (RVs), looking at their effect on overall channel behavior and on user engagement. We use data from the public YouTube Data API, which lets us control for platform, creator and video features, and this gives insights into how the YouTube ecosystem is evolving. Our analysis is longitudinal and comparative, and it quantifies changes in video content creation and user engagement across Shorts and RVs over the two years after YouTube Shorts was introduced in March 2021. The study aims to give useful insights to content creators, advertisers and researchers, so they can better understand the perspectives of an era marked by the rise of short-form video content. To look deeper into the impact of Shorts on platform content and user engagement, we address these research questions:

- RQ1 How did the introduction of Shorts affect preexisting channels in terms of content creation behavior, and how do channels created after Shorts introduction differ from older channels?

- RQ2 How do Shorts compare to RVs in terms of views and content creation frequency across video categories?

- RQ3 What differences between Shorts and RVs can be observed in terms of user engagement (views, likes, and comments), and does the duration of RVs have an influence?

Our dataset has data about 70k channels that created at least one video in the Shorts format since March 2021. We collected metadata of 9.9M Shorts and 6.9M RVs that these channels posted between January 2021 and December 2022, so we could analyze both the time around the introduction of Shorts and the long-lasting impact it had on the channels and their videos. For each video we also got its category and its number of views, likes and comments.

Our results show three main trends. First, channels that posted at least one Shorts tended to adopt the format, and eventually they uploaded more Shorts than RVs. Second, categories are not distributed evenly between Shorts and RVs: Shorts were uploaded mainly in categories related to entertainment, while RVs covered a wide variety of content, including political or educational. This means the two types of videos are not made to cover the same themes, but rather they co-exist on the platform for different purposes. Also, political, educational and artistic Shorts get fewer views, which suggests that for some categories viewers prefer RVs. Overall, Shorts did better than RVs in views and likes per view, but got fewer comments per view, although this gap is getting smaller. This trend is even stronger when we compare the engagement metrics of Shorts and RVs uploaded by the same channel, where Shorts get 110 times more views (on average) than the RVs. But when we split RVs into different duration groups, we found that the median number of views of videos from 10 to 30 minutes long was higher than the median number of views of Shorts.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 describes how we collected and processed the data. Section 3 shows how video publishing behavior changed over the observation period. Section 4 reports the content differences between Shorts and RVs. Section 5 describes how users engaged with both types of videos in terms of views, likes and comments. Section 6 discusses the impact of the introduction of Shorts on overall content publishing behavior and user reaction. Section 7 gives the prior literature on the topic. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper with its main findings, discusses limitations and gives future directions of research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
During the last few years, short-form video content has gained widespread popularity [1,2]. TikTok, a social media platform launched in 2016 that focuses on short videos, quickly became a commercial success, with 3 billion downloads and 1 billion active monthly users in 2023 [3]. Shortly after, platforms such as YouTube, Instagram and Facebook introduced their own short-form video content features, with a similar format across all platforms. YouTube, in particular, introduced its so-called Shorts format as a beta version in the US on March 18, 2021 [4], and worldwide a few months later. Since its introduction on YouTube, more and more content creators have started to produce content in this format [2].

Short-form video content is currently a topic of lively discussion, with a spectrum of perspectives. On the one hand, it gives creators an opportunity to engage and entertain their audience with concise and attractive content. Moreover, short-form videos can be effective at disseminating information about social issues [5] and create new professional perspectives for content creators [6]. On the other hand, recent studies of TikTok highlighted some potentially concerning aspects for its users, such as a form of dependency [7], an increase in daytime fatigue [8] and a decrease in prospective memory [9]. Moreover, its impact on informative content, for example educational videos that thrive on depth and detail, should be explored. To investigate this, we focus on a fundamental research question: "Are short videos replacing longer videos on YouTube, the most popular online video-sharing platform?"

To address this question, we undertake the first comprehensive study of YouTube Shorts, comparing them with regular videos (RVs) in terms of their effect on overall channel behavior and user engagement. Using data from the public YouTube Data API [10], we are able to control for platform, creator and video features, offering insights into the evolving YouTube ecosystem. Our longitudinal comparative analysis quantifies changes in video content creation and user engagement across Shorts and RVs over the two years following the introduction of YouTube Shorts in March 2021. This study aims to provide valuable insights to content creators, advertisers and researchers, helping them better understand the perspectives of an era marked by the rise of short-form video content. To delve deeper into the impact of Shorts on platform content and user engagement, we address the following research questions:

- RQ1 How did the introduction of Shorts affect preexisting channels in terms of content creation behavior, and how do channels created after Shorts introduction differ from older channels?

- RQ2 How do Shorts compare to RVs in terms of views and content creation frequency across video categories?

- RQ3 What differences between Shorts and RVs can be observed in terms of user engagement (views, likes, and comments), and does the duration of RVs have an influence?

Our dataset contains data about 70k channels that have created at least one video in the Shorts format since March 2021. We collected metadata of 9.9M Shorts and 6.9M RVs posted by those channels between January 2021 and December 2022, which allowed us to analyze both the time window around the introduction of Shorts and its long-lasting impact on those channels and their videos. For each video, we also retrieved its category and its number of views, likes and comments.

Our results highlight three main trends. First, we observed that channels that posted at least one Shorts tended to adopt the format, eventually uploading more Shorts than RVs. Second, we found that categories are not distributed evenly between Shorts and RVs: Shorts were mainly uploaded in entertainment-related categories, while RVs covered a wide variety of content, including political or educational. This indicates that the two types of videos are not created to cover the same themes, but rather co-exist on the platform for different purposes. Additionally, political, educational and artistic Shorts generate fewer views, suggesting that viewers prefer RVs for some categories. Overall, we found that Shorts outperformed RVs in terms of views and likes per view, but generated fewer comments per view, although this gap is narrowing. This trend is even more pronounced when comparing the engagement metrics of Shorts and RVs uploaded by the same channel, with Shorts getting 110 times more views (on average) than their RV counterparts. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes how we collected and processed the data used in this article. Section 3 shows how video publishing behavior evolved over the observation period. Section 4 reports the differences in content between Shorts and RVs. Section 5 describes how users engaged with both types of videos in terms of views, likes and comments. Section 6 discusses the impact of the introduction of Shorts on overall content publishing behavior and user reaction. Section 7 reviews the prior literature on the topic. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper with its main findings, discusses its limitations and provides future research directions.
